newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists await Socialist policy reply - Hue.
newsitem.headline: French Communists await Socialist policy reply - Hue.

text.p: French Communists said on Monday they wanted in principle to join a new Socialist-led cabinet but were trying to win policy commitments from Prime Minister-designate Lionel Jospin.

Party chief Robert Hue, who now holds the balance of power in the National Assembly after the left's stunning gains in Sunday's election runoff, said the party's policy-making national council had agreed Communists should serve in the new government as long as policy questions could be resolved.

"At this time we are taking action to get Lionel Jospin and the Socialist Party to give undertakings," Hue told a news conference. He said he had written to Jospin earlier in the day seeking policy clarification following private talks they had on the last day of campaigning last week.
The national committee is to discuss its proposal again on Tuesday after it has been put to grassroots Communist organisations on Monday evening.

The Communists, who won 38 of the Assembly's 577 seats to 274 for the non-Communist left, were quick to repeat demands to their Socialist allies, including relaxation of national budget criteria set for joining the planned single European currency.
National Committee member Pierre Zarka told France Inter radio that the demands were drawn from a pre-election declaration setting out a Socialist-Communist poll alliance.

He said they included "how to relax the Maastricht grip so that we no longer suffer external constraints and free ourselves from criteria that are absolutely tragic for the population and the economy".

The 1992 Maastricht Treaty set a course for deeper European political and monetary union, including strict terms for a country's qualification for the euro single currency, due to be launched in 1999.
Other demands included wage rises to trigger a consumer-led economic recovery and cutting the working week from 39 hours to 35 hours in order to slash record 12.8 percent unemployment.
"We have put precise questions and we expect answers," Zarka said.
Jospin favours a gradual approach to increasing purchasing power, including through tax reforms, while the Communists seek immediate hikes for the low-paid.
"We are not asking for the impossible...We only want universal suffrage to be heard," Zarka said.
"I cannot imagine for a minute that the Socialist Party can turn a deaf ear to the French people's expectations," he added.

A Sofres opinion poll published in the daily Le Monde said what voters mostly hoped for from a left-wing government were jobs for young people and wage hikes. Cuts in working hours and a halt to privatisations came much lower down the list.
Zarka indicated that the Communists would play an active role if they joined a Socialist-led government.
"Since we want the voice of this country's men and women to be heard in government meetings, we will not be there only as extras," he said.

The Communist leadership is divided over joining the cabinet, with the old guard remembering how participating in a Socialist-led government under the late president Francois Mitterrand in 1981-1984 precipitated their party's decline.

The Communists, who held four relatively minor portfolios, quit the cabinet after Mitterrand dropped expansionary policies for monetary orthodoxy. Their voters held them co-responsible for austerity policies and punished them in the 1986 election.
While the Communists have a potentially pivotal role in parliament, they may not have much leverage over the policies of a Socialist-led government.
The French Constitution gives the government broad powers to legislate by decree or use confidence motions to ram legislation through a recalcitrant parliament.
In a similar situation in 1988-93, minority Socialist governments relied on the Communists to support bills or abstain.

Analysts say Communists, who on Sunday won more Assembly seats than in any election since 1981, would think twice before backing a right-wing bid to bring down the government and cause another early election.

The Sofres poll said 60 percent of voters believed "cohabitation" between Jospin and conservative President Jacques Chirac would not last through the assembly's five-year term. The Constitution allows Chirac to dissolve parliament again after one year.
